title: Goroutines and channels: unbuffered, close, ranging
summary: A goroutine is a concurrently running function; a channel passes values between goroutines. An unbuffered channel is a handoff: both sides wait until the value changes hands.

examples.title: Three workers receiving from one channel
examples.nondeterminism_note: Which worker takes which job is the scheduler's decision and varies run to run. Sorted-lines comparison makes the check about the *set* of events: every job 1-6 handed to some worker, each exactly once. Output is also post-sorted in the example itself for a fully stable lesson view.

annotations.note: Launching three goroutines is just `go f()`. Each runs the same loop; the runtime schedules them on OS threads for you.
An unbuffered channel send blocks until a receiver takes the value: the sender knows the work was handed off, unlike a queue drop.
Close signals "no more values". The range loop ends when the channel is closed AND drained. Only the sender should close: a send on a closed channel panics, and so does closing it twice.

wg.Wait() blocks until the counter hits zero. The counter was incremented before `go` ran the goroutine — decrementing happens in the goroutine. Workers share the map only to collect results, under a mutex; the channel itself passed each job to exactly one worker.

use_cases: Fan-out work across workers while results stream back through a channel
Signaling completion (close a done channel) without locks
strengths: Goroutines are cheap (KB-scale stacks): thousands are normal, unlike Java's thread-per-request
Channels pass ownership of data between goroutines: no lock to forget
The compiler checks send/receive direction in typed channels
weaknesses: Wrong ownership (who closes, who reads) produces deadlocks or panics at runtime, not compile time
A nil channel blocks forever; a send on a closed channel panics
Unbuffered channels couple sender to receiver timing; sometimes you want a buffer

pitfalls.title: Closing a channel from the receiver side
pitfalls.detail: The sender then panics on send. Close belongs to the sender: it means 'I will send no more'.

pitfalls.title: Forgetting wg.Wait() or leaking goroutines
pitfalls.detail: main returning kills all goroutines instantly, half-finished. Use WaitGroup or range over the channel.

pitfalls.title: Sharing a variable across goroutines instead of sending it
pitfalls.detail: Concurrent map writes and read/write races are real. Race detector: go test -race.

quiz.q: What does a receive from a closed channel yield after it is drained?
quiz.why: Closed + drained channels return zero values with ok=false; that's how range terminates.
Close means 'no more sends coming', which only the sender can know.

body:
## Concept

`go f()` starts a goroutine: a function running concurrently with the caller. Channels are
typed conduits: `ch <- v` sends, `v := <-ch` receives. An unbuffered channel makes both
sides wait for the handoff; a closed channel signals "no more values", and `for v := range ch`
ends when the channel closes.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: goroutines ≈ virtual threads; channels ≈ BlockingQueue, but first-class in the
  language with select (later lesson) and no checked InterruptedException.
- C/C++: no mutex to forget, no data race through the channel — the value itself moves.
- JS: like posting messages to a Web Worker, but with shared memory processes cheaply and
  many goroutines instead of two isolated heaps.

## Design notes

Share memory by communicating: send the data, don't guard it with a mutex when ownership
actually transfers. A useful rule this lesson plants: whoever *sends* owns the channel and
closes it; receivers only read. When several senders exist, wrap close in a sync.Once or
collect via WaitGroup first — covered in the sync lesson.
